title: Clontarf's historic fishing sheds and Vernon Avenue
status_label: DOCUMENTED HISTORICAL CONTEXT
summary: Official historical material describes an early Clontarf fishing settlement with herring sheds fronting the Coast Road, and identifies Vernon Avenue as developing northward from the route by the sheds.
supported: Dublin City Council's 2026 Vernon Avenue preliminary design report supports the broad relationship between the herring-shed cluster, Coast Road and the avenue's origins. A specialist street-history article transcribes an 1836 Ordnance Survey Name Book description and discusses an earlier Green Lane name.
limits: The exact shed footprints and the precise route alignment have not been established. The 1836 wording and the 1816 Green Lane label remain secondary-source transcriptions until the original Name Book and Taylor map are inspected.

title: 1792 manuscript survey: Slip Field near Clontarf
status_label: PRIMARY-SOURCE LEAD · IMAGE NOT INSPECTED
summary: The National Library of Ireland catalogue records a 1792 survey by John Brownrigg, titled A survey of a piece of ground called the Slip field near Clontarf. Call number MS 21 F. 51 / (081), scale 10 perches to an inch.
supported: The manuscript map's title, date, surveyor, scale and catalogue identifier are recorded by the NLI. The catalogue says a digital copy exists.
limits: The image has not been visually inspected. 'Near Clontarf' does not establish that this field depicts the fishing sheds, Coast Road or Vernon Avenue. No map geometry or pin is inferred.

title: 1792 manuscript map: Bay View & Mount Pleasant
status_label: REGIONAL COMPARISON LEAD · IMAGE NOT INSPECTED
summary: A second John Brownrigg manuscript map in the NLI Longfield Map Collection is titled A map of Bay View & Mount Pleasant in the Barony of Coolock & County of Dublin belonging to Robert Burton Esq., dated 1792. Call number MS 21 F. 51 / (079).
supported: The NLI catalogue identifies the title, creator, date, collection and scale of 10 perches to an inch.
limits: Its precise geographic extent and relationship to the historic Clontarf sheds remain unknown until the image is inspected. It is not currently a confirmed sheds location.

title: Taylor's 1816 map and the reported Green Lane name
status_label: PRIMARY MAP INSPECTION PENDING
summary: Taylor's Map of the Environs of Dublin, Extending 10 to 14 Miles from the Castle, was published in 1816. UCD Library identifies the National Library of Scotland record, while the Vernon Avenue street-history article also cites the Virtual Treasury of Ireland catalogue item LBC-GJ-13-2 as an access route.
supported: The map's identity and date are supported by the catalogue and UCD Library guide. A secondary street-history article reports that the route was labelled Green Lane and cites the Virtual Treasury catalogue item LBC-GJ-13-2 for Taylor's map.
limits: The Clontarf portion of the 1816 map has not yet been visually inspected. The Green Lane label remains a secondary-source claim, not a direct reading of the original map. The Virtual Treasury page was reachable as a catalogue URL in this investigation, but its map image or Clontarf sheet was not extracted or inspected.

title: Rocque's Dublin maps: three dates, distinct works
status_label: MAP EDITION IDENTIFICATION IN PROGRESS
summary: The 1756, 1757 and 1760 Rocque maps are distinct publications and should not be treated as interchangeable. The Vernon Avenue secondary article itself has a date/footnote mismatch, while Dublin City Council labels its reproduced map 1757.
supported: UCD Library and the Dictionary of Irish Biography distinguish several Rocque titles and dates. Dublin City Council's 2026 report labels its reproduced map 1757.
limits: The exact original sheet behind each modern reference has not yet been identified. No claim is made that a particular Rocque sheet proves the location of individual sheds.

title: The 1836 Ordnance Survey Name Book: primary entry still to inspect
status_label: PRIMARY RECORD ACCESS TARGET
summary: The NLI catalogue lists four typed-copy volumes of the County Dublin Ordnance Survey Name Books. Volume I, call number BB6442, covers Aderrig to Coolock and is the correct volume to investigate for Clontarf.
supported: The County Dublin collection is separate from the digitised City of Dublin compilation. The 1836 wording about a road through 'The Sheds of Clontarf Village' is currently known through a secondary article.
limits: The original County Name Book entry has not been directly inspected. The City of Dublin Name Book PDF is not a substitute for the County volume.

title: 1837: contemporary description of the Clontarf sheds
status_label: CONTEMPORARY PRINTED SOURCE · DIRECT TEXT INSPECTED
summary: Samuel Lewis's 1837 Topographical Dictionary describes wooden buildings along Clontarf's water edge, called the Clontarf sheds and formerly used to cure fish. It also records a profitable oyster bank off the sheds.
supported: The digitised 1837 parish entry explicitly links the Clontarf sheds to the coastal edge and fish curing. It places an oyster bank offshore from the sheds. This is strong contemporary printed evidence for the fishing-sheds locality and its maritime economy.
limits: The text does not give a surveyed boundary, the number or footprints of individual sheds, or an exact modern coordinate. 'Along the water's edge' must not be converted into a precise map polygon.

title: 1792: Patrick Toole's will abstract names the Sheds of Clontarf
status_label: PUBLISHED ARCHIVAL ABSTRACT · UNDERLYING RECORD NOT INSPECTED
summary: The Irish Manuscripts Commission's digitised Registry of Deeds Abstracts of Wills, Volume III, identifies Patrick Toole's property in the Sheds of Clontarf and a dwellinghouse in the Green of the Sheds. The entry is dated 11 September 1792, not 1789.
supported: The searchable published abstract identifies Patrick Toole, Sheds of Clontarf, County Dublin, and the date 11 September 1792. It refers to leasehold and other property in the Sheds and a dwellinghouse in the Green of the Sheds.
limits: The original memorial/deed has not been inspected directly. The abstract does not identify a precise plot, establish the physical location of the house, or map any shed footprints. Earlier project metadata incorrectly dated this entry 1789; that error is corrected in this update.

title: A reported 1728 map label: “Herring Sheds” at Clontarf
status_label: SECONDARY MAP TRANSCRIPTION · ORIGINAL IMAGE CHECK PENDING
summary: Dillon Cosgrave's local-history account states that Captain Perry's 1728 Map of Dublin Bay and Harbour marks “Herring Sheds” at the coast road below Vernon Avenue.
supported: The published chapter explicitly attributes the label to the 1728 map and places it at the Clontarf Sheds locality. The Dublin Port Archive catalogue independently identifies a 1728 map titled A New and Correct Map of the Bay and Harbour of Dublin with a small Plan of the City.
limits: The original map label and its exact position have not been independently read from the map image. Do not treat this secondary transcription as a georeferenced point or proof of exact shed geometry. The map's provenance and reproduction permissions must be respected.

title: 1785: a print titled The Sheds of Clontarfe
status_label: BRITISH LIBRARY PRINT IDENTIFIED · IMAGE INSPECTION PENDING
summary: The British Library's King's Topographical Collection inventory lists an 1785 print titled The Sheds of Clontarfe, by Thomas Malton after Francis Wheatley, shelfmark Maps K.Top.53.25. This is a direct visual-source lead specifically titled for the Clontarf sheds.
supported: The catalogue inventory gives the title, maker attribution, date and British Library shelfmark. A digitised dictionary of Irish artists also records Malton's 1785 aquatint after Wheatley.
limits: The print image has not yet been inspected at adequate resolution. We cannot yet describe buildings, shoreline, viewpoint or exact geography from its title alone. The higher-quality scan and reproduction terms need to be obtained from the British Library.

title: 1704: an early survey of the Parish of Clontarf
status_label: MANUSCRIPT MAP CATALOGUED · COVERAGE OF SHEDS UNCHECKED
summary: A 1704 survey by John Greene Junior is catalogued by the Virtual Treasury as a map of lands in the Barony of Coolock and Parish of Clontarf. Its stated boundaries include the Strand and Upper Hollybrook.
supported: The Virtual Treasury catalogue provides the map's date, creator, reference code DCLA C1 S1/130 and boundary description. This establishes a useful early cadastral source for the wider parish.
limits: The map image has not yet been inspected to establish whether it covers the Sheds or the relevant shoreline. Its title and parish-wide scope do not prove that the Sheds appear on the sheet. No map geometry or pin is inferred.

title: A possible earlier name: Herringtowne, 1693
status_label: SECONDARY HISTORICAL CLAIM · ORIGINAL CHART INSPECTION PENDING
summary: A Clontarf historical report states that the Sheds fishing-port was referred to as Herringtowne in Greenville Collins' 1693 map of the area.
supported: The secondary report explicitly attributes the name Herringtowne to Collins' 1693 map. This creates an earlier name-search lead for the fishing settlement.
limits: The original chart and exact label have not been inspected. Do not treat Herringtowne as a verified map transcription or assume that it labels precisely the same footprint later called the Sheds.

title: 1786: Christmas Weekes and water supply at Clontarf
status_label: HISTORICAL LETTER TRANSCRIPTION · ORIGINAL RECORD PENDING
summary: A published transcription reproduces a 30 November 1786 letter from Christmas Weekes at Clontarf thanking the County Grand Jury for recognition of works supplying shipping with water and other uses.
supported: The transcription identifies Weekes, Clontarf, the date and the subject of water-supply works. This may add an infrastructure strand to the story of the Sheds and the coastal settlement.
limits: The original Grand Jury record has not been inspected. The letter does not establish a precise pipe route, exact location of a water source or individual shed locations.

title: Bottlemaker's Hall survives as a protected former workers' club; 2026 planning application documents its reuse proposal
status_label: CURRENT PLANNING EVIDENCE · FOUNDER FIELD PHOTOGRAPHY PENDING
summary: Bottlemaker's Hall (also known as Dolphin House) is recorded as a 1915 club building for the Irish Glass Bottlemakers' Society. Dublin City Council's current RPS lists it as RPS 4003. A 2026 planning application describes the existing vacant 250 m² complex and proposes renovation and conversion.
supported: The Dictionary of Irish Architects identifies Aubrey Vincent O'Rourke as architect, John Dillon as builder and 1915 as the date. Dublin City Council's Ringsend & Irishtown Walking Trail corroborates the date and social history. The current statutory RPS includes Bottlemaker's Hall as RPS 4003. The 2026 planning application WEB3596/26 describes the extant building complex, its former social-club and manager's-apartment uses, rear dancehall and proposed repair works.
limits: The planning application is undecided in the source checked and must not be represented as permission granted or works completed. The map coordinate is an approximate planning-site marker, not a surveyed building point or founder GPS. Current visible condition, exact fabric survival, architectural details and lawful photography viewpoints require founder fieldwork. The property is not open for casual access.

title: Ringsend RPS 7378–7381: distinguish the surviving tramway powerhouse from unverified gate and entrance features
area: RINGSEND ROAD · GRAND CANAL DOCK · DUBLIN 4
status_label: RPS LISTINGS CHECKED · POWERHOUSE IDENTITY CORROBORATED · OTHER FEATURES UNRESOLVED
summary: Dublin City Council's current RPS lists the former Reg Armstrong Works entrance (7378), the former Irish Glass Bottle Company office (7379), four CIE bus-depot granite gate piers (7380), and the Ringsend Shelbourne Pierrot Club / former Bovril building (7381). New research identifies the physical building at 20 Ringsend Road, now Windmill Lane Recording Studios, as the former Dublin United Tramways Company electrical powerhouse, built in 1932.
supported: The current DCC RPS Volume 4 confirms the four entries and their register descriptions. Windmill Lane Recording Studios' own building-history page and 2020 press release state that 20 Ringsend Road was the electrical power station for the tramline depot and that the studios moved to the protected Art Deco building in 1990. Archiseek identifies the building as the 1932 DUTC Powerhouse by Vincent Kelly and notes that its Art Deco piers and sun-ray gates are missing. The building was added to the physical catalogue as DUB-BLD-0095.
limits: The short RPS 7381 description uses the former Shelbourne Pierrot Club / Bovril building name, while the current occupier documents the same 20 Ringsend Road building as a tramway powerhouse. These are treated as layered uses of one building, but the exact chronology and details of the Bovril phase need archival confirmation. RPS 7378's classical cut-stone carriage entrance and RPS 7380's four granite gate piers have not yet been independently confirmed as physically extant in 2026; no map pins were created for them. RPS 7379's former Irish Glass Bottle Company office remains separate from the demolished factory investigated in Batch 101; the office's present fabric and survival still need confirmation. The OSM building point for 20 Ringsend Road is source-derived, not founder GPS.

title: Poolbeg Lighthouse and the protected Pigeon House / Great South Wall heritage landscape
area: POOLBEG PENINSULA · PIGEON HOUSE HARBOUR · GREAT SOUTH WALL · DUBLIN 4
status_label: POOLBEG LIGHTHOUSE CATALOGUED · PIGEON HOUSE PRECINCT REQUIRES SURVIVAL AND ACCESS VERIFICATION
summary: The research adds Poolbeg Lighthouse as a separately documented physical object and opens a wider investigation of the Pigeon House heritage landscape. Dublin City Council's current RPS identifies the former St Catherine's Hospital remains (6793), remnants of Pigeon House Fort (6794), former Pigeon House Hotel (6795), former red-brick Pigeon House power station (6796), sea walls along Pigeon House Road (6797), and the Great South Wall to the lighthouse (6798).
supported: Dublin Port records that Poolbeg Lighthouse was first lit on 29 September 1767, replacing a floating light at the end of the South Bull Wall. The Dictionary of Irish Architects records John Smyth's responsibility for the lighthouse's construction in 1766–1767 and the eastern abutment of the South Wall in or after 1771. The exact-object photograph by David Dixon, captured 21 June 2018 and visually inspected on Wikimedia Commons, carries an explicit CC BY-SA 2.0 licence and records the depicted lighthouse position at 53.342128, -6.151459. The lighthouse is catalogued as DUB-BLD-0096. Dublin City Film Office describes the former Pigeon House power station as built in phases 1902–03, 1911–13 and 1933–40 and decommissioned in the 1970s. An archaeological survey of Pigeon House Fort was reported in 2009 under SMR DU019-027 / licence 09E0259.
limits: The RPS descriptions establish statutory listing, not the exact present-day condition, survival or accessible extent of every feature. The 2009 fort survey documents remains at that date, not their 2026 condition. Dublin Port's Heritage Conservation Strategy describes restoring pedestrian access from Ringsend to Pigeon House Harbour via the Great South Wall as a long-term aspiration and records port security/access constraints; do not assume the Pigeon House precinct is open to the public. The modern Poolbeg Generating Station (including the 2021 trial-pit report) is distinct from the former Pigeon House Power Station (RPS 6796). No separate map pins were created for the fort, hotel, hospital remains, harbour sea walls or former power station in this batch because exact geometry, current survival and lawful access require further verification. The lighthouse coordinate is source-derived, not founder GPS. The Commons photograph is a third-party reference, not founder photography.

title: Pigeon House Hotel, Great South Wall attendant structures and Ringsend drainage / riverfront micro-heritage
area: PIGEON HOUSE PRECINCT · GREAT SOUTH WALL · RINGSEND · RIVER DODDER
status_label: FOUR SOURCE-LOCATED OBJECTS ADDED · SIGNAL TOWER AND BURIED FEATURES NOT PINNED
summary: Discovery Expansion Batch 105 uses the Dublin Port Company 3FM Environmental Impact Assessment and its illustrated Appendix 16-1 catalogue to add four separately identifiable physical objects: the former Pigeon House Hotel (RPS 6795), a c.1920–30 concrete boat slip (DCIHR 18-12-118), a c.1900 timber-and-metal landing stage (DCIHR 18-12-121), and a c.1900 stone syphon house (DCIHR 18-12-151-01). Each has a published ITM point transformed to WGS84; none is represented as founder field GPS.
supported: The Dublin City Film Office records the Pigeon House Hotel as built 1793–1795, a classical dressed-ashlar granite building of three storeys over basement. The 3FM EIAR identifies RPS 6795 as standing and supplies ITM 720343, 733686. The same report describes the boat slip's concrete construction, iron railings/posts, mooring blocks, cast-iron lamp and adjacent limestone quay wall; it describes the landing stage's timber deck and metal frame, disused and in disrepair; and it gives a detailed architectural description of the disused stone syphon house. The hotel and three smaller structures are registered as distinct records DUB-BLD-0097 and DUB-INF-0006 to DUB-INF-0008.
limits: The EIAR is a project assessment with site inspections and an asset catalogue, but its survey snapshot does not prove unchanged condition or access in November 2026. The hotel is not a public attraction; March 2026 local reporting describes a council letting proposal and use by a wastewater operator, but this is not the executed lease. The EIAR's embedded photographs were not imported because image-specific reuse rights were not established. The Pigeon House Fort Signal Tower (RMP DU019-038001) is described in the EIAR as standing and buried but its location is expressly approximate; no pin or catalogue object is created until its footprint is independently reconciled. The Blockhouse is listed as a site rather than a standing building. Macerals Slip (DCIHR 19-09-001) is recorded as buried beneath the container terminal and is not a present-day visible-object pin. The report also documents the Pigeon House Harbour walls and basin, but their exact extent and current physical condition need further assessment. No authoritative source confirming a separate lifeboat house was established in this batch; it remains an unverified search lead, not an archive fact. The historic St Catherine's Hospital boundary remains and the former Pigeon House power station remain separate assets requiring exact extent/current condition/access checks.

title: Half Moon Battery, former Lifeboat House remains and South Wall Sluice House
area: GREAT SOUTH WALL · POOLBEG PENINSULA · DUBLIN 4
status_label: THREE ASSETS CATALOGUED · FIELD PHOTOGRAPHY AND ACCESS CHECK REQUIRED
summary: Batch 106 uses Dublin Port Company's 3FM EIAR Appendix 16-1 to catalogue three separately referenced heritage assets: Half Moon Battery (RMP DU019-028), the former Lifeboat House site (DCIHR 19-09-008), and the South Wall Sluice House (DCIHR 19-09-009-01). Each has an ITM point transformed to WGS84 and a founder photography brief.
supported: Appendix 16-1 describes Half Moon Battery as a 1793 gun battery with a surviving south-facing granite perimeter wall, a possible gun-swivel curvature in the Great South Wall and a stone slipway; the report gives ITM 722275, 733893. It describes the Lifeboat House as a c.1850 site with red-brick and granite wall stubs, a breached concrete enclosure wall and ruinous perimeter path; ITM 721370, 733814. It describes the Sluice House as a detached three-bay single-storey masonry building built c.1881, with rubble-stone walls, rusticated quoins and blocked window openings; ITM 721427, 733833. The catalogue explains that entries draw on statutory registers, industrial heritage records, port archives and project field walkover inspections.
limits: The 3FM EIAR Appendix 16-1 calls Half Moon Battery a five-gun battery armed with five 24-pounder guns, while Dublin Port's Heritage Conservation Strategy describes a three-gun platform battery. The discrepancy is preserved for further archival checking. The Lifeboat House is catalogued as a site, not a complete standing building; the EIAR describes wall stubs and enclosure remnants. The sluice house is described as abandoned at survey date. None of these survey descriptions proves unchanged condition or current public access in November 2026. The source PDF's photographs were not copied into the visual register because image-specific reuse rights were not independently established. All three new visual records await founder photography.

title: Two c.1770 masonry landing slips on the Great South Wall
area: PIGEON HOUSE FORT EASTERN ENTRANCE · WHITE BANK WHARF · GREAT SOUTH WALL · DUBLIN 4
status_label: TWO SOURCE-LOCATED MASONRY SLIPS ADDED · FIELD VERIFICATION REQUIRED
summary: Further review of Dublin Port Company's 3FM EIAR Appendix 16-1 identifies two separate historic masonry slipways: the landing slip beside the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort (DCIHR 19-09-012) and the White Bank Wharf South Wall slip (DCIHR 19-09-011). Both are associated with the Great South Wall and have separate source-derived ITM points.
supported: Appendix 16-1 describes DCIHR 19-09-012 as a c.1770 masonry boat slip, approximately 25m by 4.3m, with rectangular granite blocks, stepped profile and up to four visible courses; ITM 720462, 733814. It describes DCIHR 19-09-011 as a slip believed c.1770, integrated into the Great South Wall, with long rectangular blocks laid at right angles to the wall; its north-west corner had suffered erosion and partial collapse; ITM 721402, 733860. limits: The report is a survey snapshot and does not prove unchanged condition in November 2026. The eastern Pigeon House Fort slip is within a port landscape where access restrictions apply, and the report notes sheet piles and foreshore conditions. The White Bank slip is exposed to tidal and shipping wash and has recorded erosion/collapse. Coordinates are transformed from report ITM points, not founder GPS. No embedded report photographs were imported because image-specific reuse rights were not independently established.

title: Dublin Port Graving Dock No. 2 — NIAH date and present-condition discrepancy
status_label: OFFICIAL-SOURCE CONFLICT · FURTHER IDENTITY CHECK REQUIRED
summary: NIAH Registration 50060588 describes a c.1910 concrete graving dock and says it remains in use. Dublin Port's heritage account identifies Graving Dock No. 2 as opening in 1957 and states that it was infilled in 2021 to create a public plaza. The available descriptions may refer to different dock phases or contain a stale NIAH use/date field.
supported: The NIAH record supplies registration 50060588, a site coordinate, a c.1910 date, concrete construction, sluice gates and cast-iron mechanisms. Dublin Port's official Pumphouse page gives the dock chronology and states Dock No. 2 opened in 1957 and closed in 2017. Dublin Port Archive describes the 2021 infill and retention of dock-gate features.
limits: The exact physical identity and footprint correspondence between NIAH 50060588 and Dublin Port's Graving Dock No. 2 have not been established. The date discrepancy is unresolved. No current dock chamber or operational use is asserted, and no separate catalogue pin is created until the NIAH and port plans are cross-referenced.

title: Pumphouse No. 2, buried 1728 sea wall, 1826 patent slip and Graving Dock No. 2 fabric
area: ALEXANDRA BASIN · EAST WALL ROAD · DUBLIN 1
status_label: OFFICIAL HERITAGE EVIDENCE · EXACT FOOTPRINTS / PRESENT STATE REQUIRE CHECK
summary: Dublin Port's Conservation Strategy identifies a second pumphouse built in the 1950s, associated with Graving Dock No. 2, with electrically driven pumps and substantial underground structure. The same strategy records the 1826 patent slip as uncovered and recovered, and an electric capstan associated with Graving Dock No. 2 as recorded during the redevelopment. Dublin Port's Substation account records a section of the original 1728 sea wall discovered beneath the substation during refurbishment. These are distinct heritage subjects, but their exact present locations, visibility and access are not sufficiently established for separate public map pins in this batch.
supported: The Conservation Strategy (PDF pp. 122 and 125) describes Pumphouse No. 2, the Graving Dock No. 2 infill in 2021, the 1826 patent slip recovery and the electric capstan recording. Dublin Port's official Substation history describes the discovery of part of the 1728 sea wall beneath the substation and states that facing stones were likely reused in the visible boundary wall.
limits: The exact footprint and surviving above-ground extent of Pumphouse No. 2 have not yet been georeferenced against a reliable site plan. The 1826 patent slip was recovered and samples of its stones taken into care; its original alignment and current storage location are not established by the consulted public source. The electric capstan was recorded during works, but its present disposition and exact position are not confirmed. The 1728 sea wall is described as a buried discovery; the suggested reuse of facing stones in the boundary wall is explicitly only likely. Do not create speculative map pins or assert that any of these features are visible to visitors.

title: Odlum's Mills and R. & H. Hall — west Dublin Port grain-storage complex
area: ALEXANDRA ROAD · BRANCH ROAD SOUTH · DUBLIN 1
status_label: FOUR NIAH RECORDS · SOURCE-DERIVED LOCATORS
summary: Four separately registered NIAH industrial buildings at the west end of Dublin Port form a documented grain-storage landscape: the monumental R. & H. Hall silo (50060589), two Odlum's Mills silo structures (50060590 and 50060591), and a separate early steel-frame redbrick industrial building on Alexandra Road (50060592). The NIAH descriptions identify reinforced-concrete silos, riveted steel silo drums, a riveted iron structural frame, loading features and early twentieth-century industrial design.
supported: Each building has its own NIAH registration, description and Irish Grid coordinate. Dublin Port's Conservation Strategy explicitly includes the former Odlums Flour Mills among the heritage assets within its conservation strategy. The R. & H. Hall entry records its previous name as Merchants Warehousing Company Ltd/Odlum's Mills; the separate Odlum's records describe neighbouring structures. The buildings are therefore recorded as separate objects rather than merged into a single invented structure.
limits: NIAH coordinates have been transformed to WGS 84 and are source-derived, not founder GPS. The exact current operational status, ownership boundaries, access rights and safe public viewpoints have not been field-verified. The term 'Odlum's Mills complex' is used as group context, not as a claim that every registered building had identical ownership or function at every date. The industrial port is operational; no public access or interior access is implied.

title: Port Centre, Alexandra Road reconstruction and North Wall freight-rail continuity
area: EAST WALL ROAD · ALEXANDRA ROAD · NORTH WALL · DUBLIN 1 / DUBLIN 3
status_label: OFFICIAL HERITAGE REGISTER + PORT INFRASTRUCTURE UPDATES
summary: Port Centre (NIAH 50120265) is a separately registered late-twentieth-century architectural landmark at the entrance to Dublin Port. Dublin Port's project updates document the reconstruction of Alexandra Road and its integrated rail line, including new rail turnouts, a pedestrian/cycle path and utility ducting. A separate 2025 update records a €9 million North Wall freight-yard upgrade to support rail freight during the Alexandra Road works, with direct rail access to the port anticipated to resume in 2027.
supported: The NIAH record gives Port Centre's architect, design competition history, construction dates, architectural description and Irish Grid coordinate. Dublin Port's Alexandra Road project page describes the road/rail works and a closure period stated as 19 July 2025 to Autumn 2026. Dublin Port's 6 June 2025 release confirms the North Wall rail freight yard investment and states the anticipated 2027 return of direct rail access into the Port.
limits: The Alexandra Road page's stated closure period has passed by the research date, but the consulted page does not confirm whether the road and rail line have reopened. The 2027 direct-access statement is a forecast, not proof of completed work. No exact historical track alignment, individual turnout coordinate or surviving rail component is inferred from these current project updates. The North Wall freight yard is operational infrastructure and is not represented as a visitor attraction.

title: North Wall Quay — surviving mooring fittings, recessed ladders and historic travelling-crane rail drawings
area: NORTH WALL QUAY · BETWEEN CONVENTION CENTRE AND NEW WAPPING STREET · DUBLIN 1
status_label: TWO SUB-FEATURES CATALOGUED · CRANE-RAIL PLAN LEAD
summary: NIAH Registration 50010011 describes paired iron mooring hooks set into the granite coping and three shallow recesses containing iron ladders on the c.1800 North Wall Quay wall. These two feature groups are now separately catalogued beneath the existing quay-wall record, without invented individual coordinates. Dublin Port Archive's engineering-drawings catalogue also lists an 1881 plan and section for the arrangement of rail in connection with travelling cranes at North Wall Goods Terminus (ED/5074), alongside a c.1890 North Wall Quay cross-section and old quay-wall plan (ED/8853).
supported: The NIAH record explicitly describes the mooring hooks and three ladder recesses. The Dublin Port Archive collection page explicitly lists drawing ED/5074 by Chris Mulrany (1881) and drawing ED/8853 (c.1890). These sources establish that the fittings are recorded on the quay and that the historical crane-rail drawing exists in the archive catalogue.
limits: The NIAH entry does not give a count or individual position for the mooring hooks, and does not provide separate coordinates for the three ladders. Current survival and condition must be field-checked. The online archive catalogue listing does not expose sufficient drawing detail to place the travelling-crane rails on the present map. No crane, rail or bollard pin is created from the catalogue title alone.

title: Dublin Port Diving Bell — Stoney's compressed-air quay construction technology and public display
status_label: NIAH REGISTER + DUBLIN PORT HISTORY + PORT ARCHIVE
summary: The Dublin Port Diving Bell is a separately registered NIAH industrial artefact (50020468), now displayed on Sir John Rogerson's Quay. It was designed by port engineer Bindon Blood Stoney and used in constructing deep-water quay walls. The bell's chamber, vertical access shaft, iron rungs and air-lock arrangement are described by NIAH; Dublin Port and its archive describe its compressed-air operation, crew, heavy precast quay blocks and use in building the North Wall Extension and Alexandra Basin.
supported: NIAH provides a dedicated registration and Irish Grid coordinate. Dublin Port's official history states delivery in 1866, entry into service in 1871 and use until 1958. Dublin Port Archive describes the bell's operation and its role in quay construction, and records its public display and later interpretive museum arrangement. Dublin Port's Distributed Museum page lists the Diving Bell as a heritage/amenity asset.
limits: The chronology varies slightly between sources: NIAH says fabricated c.1870 and used from 1872, while Dublin Port says delivered 1866 and entered service 1871. Both source-specific statements are retained. The NIAH coordinate is transformed from Irish Grid and is not founder GPS. Public exhibition is documented but current opening hours and any temporary access restrictions must be checked before visiting. The present interpretive installation includes modern supports and display infrastructure; distinguish these from the historic bell itself.

title: The Ferryman — surviving Georgian pair at 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay
area: SIR JOHN ROGERSON'S QUAY · CARDIFF LANE · DUBLIN 2
status_label: NIAH REGISTER + EIAR HERITAGE INVENTORY
summary: NIAH Registration 50020479 records The Ferryman as a corner-sited pair of attached former houses built c.1820, now in use as a public house and guest house. The building retains a documented mix of Georgian brickwork, granite details, timber sliding-sash windows and carved Portland-stone door details. The former houses also have a documented history of nineteenth-century retail and maritime trades.
supported: The NIAH record supplies the date range, architectural description, appraisal, Irish Grid reference and historical occupant/trade information. The Ringsend to City Centre Core Bus Corridor Scheme EIAR, Volume 4, Appendix A16.3, page 30 independently identifies the Ferryman at 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, c.1820, and lists Dublin City Council RPS 7549–7550.
limits: The NIAH coordinate is a source-derived site locator, not founder GPS; the underlying point accuracy is unspecified. The current condition of individual sash windows, carved details and openings has not been field-checked. No image was added because file-level reuse permission was not established. Public access to the street-facing exterior does not imply permission to enter the premises or photograph private interiors.

title: Sir John Rogerson's Quay — Catholic Seamen's Institute and Columbia Mills
status_label: TWO NIAH REGISTERS + DCC PROTECTED STRUCTURES REGISTER + PLANNING HISTORY
summary: Two further historic structures are documented on Sir John Rogerson's Quay: the c.1825 former Catholic Seamen's Institute at No. 4 (NIAH 50020472; RPS 7544), and Columbia Mills at Nos. 14–15 (NIAH 50020474; RPS 7546), a c.1890 former mill associated with H.M. Leask & Company. NIAH also records vestigial lettering associated with the former Seamen's Institute; this is separately registered as a parent-linked inscription target without an independent coordinate.
supported: The two NIAH records provide architectural descriptions, historical uses and Irish Grid references. Dublin City Council's RPS list identifies both protected structures. The 2023 Ringsend to City Centre Core Bus Corridor planning report describes the protected buildings at Nos. 4 and 5 as exceptions to demolition under a permitted redevelopment scheme. NIAH specifically records visible lettering on the platbands and vestiges of the institute sign at No. 4.
limits: The NIAH surveys date from 2015 and do not establish current condition. The planning report records a permitted scheme, not proof of completed works. No. 4 is described as disused by NIAH; its current occupancy and public access remain unconfirmed. Columbia Mills' 2020 planning appeal includes a proposed alteration and extension; the proposal must not be mistaken for completed construction. The inscription's exact wording and present survival are unknown. All coordinates are source-derived and not founder GPS.

title: Sir John Rogerson's Quay — granite steps, campshire setts and rails, and timber fenders
status_label: NIAH 50020465 · THREE PARENT-LINKED MICRO-DETAILS
summary: NIAH Registration 50020465 documents three further photographable feature groups on Sir John Rogerson's Quay: granite steps with cast-iron railings; stone setts and inset cast-iron rails to the campshire; and timber fenders north of the B.J. Marine building. These are now separately catalogued as child records beneath the existing quay-wall object, DUB-INF-0029. No independent feature coordinates or map pins have been invented.
supported: The official NIAH description for registration 50020465 explicitly lists the granite steps and railings, stone setts and inset cast-iron rails to the campshire, and timber fenders north of the B.J. Marine building. The same record dates the ashlar-granite quay wall to c.1870 and provides the wider historical and engineering context.
limits: NIAH does not supply individual feature coordinates, counts, detailed dimensions, installation dates or present-condition confirmation for these feature groups. The timber fenders are located only by reference to the B.J. Marine building. The purpose of the inset rails is not specified in the consulted record, so no crane, railway or other specific function is assigned. All three child records remain without independent map pins and await safe founder field verification.

title: Ringsend historic concrete boat slip — iron railings, mooring blocks and cast-iron lamppost
area: GREAT SOUTH WALL · RINGSEND WATERFRONT · DUBLIN 4
status_label: DCIHR 18-12-118 · THREE PARENT-LINKED MICRO-DETAILS
summary: The Dublin Port 3FM EIAR cultural-heritage catalogue describes the c.1920–30 concrete boat slip (DCIHR 18-12-118) with iron posts and railings, concrete mooring blocks, and a cast-iron lamppost at its north-west corner. These three individually photographable components are now catalogued beneath DUB-INF-0006.
supported: Appendix 16-1 identifies the boat slip as a concrete structure dating c.1920–30, records original railings, concrete mooring blocks and a cast-iron lamppost at its north-west corner, and notes the limestone masonry quay wall to the east. It states that the slip was built on the site of an earlier wooden pier shown on the 1912 OS map.
limits: The EIAR is a survey record and does not prove that every component remains in place today. It provides no individual counts, dimensions, maker details or exact coordinates for the child features. No independent coordinates or map pins have been assigned. Access is not assumed; photograph only from safe lawful public viewpoints.

title: Great South Wall and Ballast Office Wall — surviving parapets, exposed wall section and visibility gaps
area: RINGSEND · PIGEON HOUSE ROAD · POOLBEG · DUBLIN 4
status_label: 3FM HERITAGE REPORT · RMP DU018-066 / DU019-029 · RPS 6928
summary: The 3FM Great South Wall heritage report distinguishes the 1759 Ballast Office Wall from the later masonry extension towards Poolbeg. It records some Ballast Office Wall boundary sections as visible low parapets and a portion of the north-facing wall as exposed to full height along the ESB Dublin Bay Power Plant cooling-water outfall. The Great South Wall's Area 4 plan states that a significant part of the northern parapet remained intact there in the survey context, while most of the southern parapet was destroyed above ground.
supported: The report's historical account dates the Ballast Office Wall to 1759 and describes it as two parallel rubble walls with sand filling the space between. It says the alignment now lies beneath Pigeon House Road, with some boundary walls visible as low parapets. The Area 4 site plan and text locate a full-height exposed portion along the cooling-water outfall. The report separately describes the later Poolbeg extension as having a dry rubble core and granite ashlar façades. It identifies the Great South Wall as RMP DU018-066 and DU019-029 and RPS 6928.
limits: The report's diagrams and descriptions are survey/project evidence, not proof of current 2026 condition. It does not supply individual coordinates for each parapet remnant. The cooling-water outfall section is adjacent to ESB/industrial infrastructure and public access is not established. Some stretches of the Great South Wall are buried, missing above ground, behind fences or inaccessible. The Great South Wall and Ballast Office Wall are related but distinct construction phases; do not merge their fabric or dates.

title: Great South Wall parapet capping — original basalt mix, timber coping history and later repair distinctions
area: GREAT SOUTH WALL · RINGSEND TO POOLBEG · DUBLIN 4
status_label: OFFICIAL 3FM EIAR · APPENDIX 16-6 · OCTOBER 2023
summary: The 3FM conservation specification records basalt as part of the original parapet-capping material and deliberately excludes basalt from proposed rebuilt capping so that new work remains subtly distinguishable. The accompanying overview separately records historical use of timber coping in some places, most of which it says had rotted and been replaced with cement. It also warns that square stone coping found on some rebuilt areas is not original and is not the model for new reconstruction.
supported: Appendix 16-6 says original capping material contains a mix of basalt stone; for rebuilding, basalt is proposed to be omitted so the new stone texture remains discernible from original fabric. It prefers salvaged stone from areas carefully dismantled for the 3FM project, then similar stone if salvaged material is exhausted. The specification sets out NHL 3.5 lime mortar, careful recording of affected masonry, mortar analysis and repair methods. The Great South Wall Overview, historical account p.5, states timber coping was used in some places but most had rotted and been replaced with cement. Its mitigation summary pp.18–19 distinguishes original parapet profiles from later square stone coping and describes a domed capping profile for proposed reconstruction.
limits: Neither source supplies a dependable, individually georeferenced inventory of surviving basalt capping stones or surviving timber coping. The timber coping statement is historical and explicitly says most had rotted; it does not identify surviving examples. The basalt statement describes original capping composition and a proposed rebuilding distinction, not a verified current stone-by-stone survey. Square coping is identified as later/non-original in the report, but individual locations are not established here. No new physical object records or map pins are justified by this evidence alone. The engineering drawings S26-HER-XX-DR-HE 100-1000 to 1006 are referenced but were not independently inspected in this batch.

title: Great South Wall roundhead — 2026 rock-armour reinforcement at Poolbeg Lighthouse
area: POOLBEG LIGHTHOUSE · GREAT SOUTH WALL ROUNDHEAD · DUBLIN 4
status_label: DUBLIN PORT COMPANY · 23 MARCH 2026
summary: Dublin Port Company reported completion of remedial rock-armour works around the Great South Wall roundhead near Poolbeg Lighthouse. The release describes approximately 5,000 tonnes of individually sized 6–9 tonne rocks transported by barge from Arklow and placed using a 150-tonne long-reach material handler. The feature is now separately catalogued as a contemporary infrastructure detail beneath the Great South Wall.
supported: The official Port release dated 23 March 2026 states that the €2.5 million works followed storm damage, restored the breakwater's design profile, and that public access near the lighthouse had reopened after completion. It also identifies the rock sizes, total tonnage, barge transport and placement machinery.
limits: The release does not provide exact chainage, a surveyed footprint, exact number of rocks, as-built drawings or an independent post-completion condition survey. It does not establish the current condition on 11 November 2026. No coordinates or map pin are assigned. The project image is credited to Murphy and is not reused because a separate image licence was not established. This contemporary rock armour must not be described as original historic masonry.

title: St Anne’s Park — shell house and Naniken River grotto
status_label: OFFICIAL NIAH RECORDS CONSULTED
summary: Two separately catalogued landscape features in the former St Anne’s estate are documented by the NIAH: the shell house within the walled garden (50030040) and the grotto beside the Naniken River (50030035). Both are described as mid-nineteenth-century features associated with the estate landscaping.
supported: NIAH 50030040 documents shell-and-pebble decoration, bone and skull material in niches, the central pier inscription “The House that Jack built”, and a dog figure.
NIAH 50030035 documents the pointed-arch grotto, calp-limestone rubble frontage, yellow-brick groin vault and riverside setting.
Dublin City Council provides public park visitor information; this does not establish the present access condition of either individual feature.
Dublin City Council's dedicated Follies guide independently lists Shell House / Dogs Graveyard and Rustic Hermits Cave – Cave among the twelve St Anne’s Park follies.
limits: No founder field inspection has been completed.
NIAH Irish Grid references are retained, but no WGS84 point or field GPS is assigned in this batch.
Present condition, visibility, exact path approach and any temporary access restrictions remain to be checked on site.
The NIAH suggestion that the shell house decoration may have been made by or for the Guinness daughters is not treated as proven attribution.
The grotto is also described as a hermitage in the NIAH appraisal; its original function is not asserted as certain.

title: St Anne’s Park — Roman Tower, Annie Lee Tower and Bridge, and Clock Tower
status_label: THREE OFFICIAL NIAH RECORDS CONSULTED
summary: Three separately registered structures in St Anne’s Park were identified in the NIAH and checked against the existing catalogue: the Roman Tower (50030021), Annie Lee Tower and Bridge (50030023), and Clock Tower (50030037).
supported: NIAH 50030021 records the Roman Tower as built in 1837 and moved from the roof of St Anne’s House to its present position in 1873; it served as a viewing tower over Dublin Bay.
NIAH 50030023 records the Annie Lee Tower and Bridge as dating to 1838 and links its construction to the birth of Annie Lee; the plaque on the tower was inserted in 1926.
NIAH 50030037 records the Clock Tower as built in 1854 and describes its four-stage form, walled-garden entrance, clock, bell and former inscription.
Dublin City Council identifies these as part of the twelve follies in the St Anne’s Park landscape.
limits: No founder field inspection has been completed; present condition and visibility remain unverified.
NIAH Irish Grid references are retained, but no WGS84 coordinate or field GPS is assigned in this batch.
The former Clock Tower inscription is a historical source statement and is not assumed to survive.
The Annie Lee Tower plaque wording has not been transcribed without direct inspection.

title: St Anne’s Park — Herculanean Temple, rustic archway and Yew Circle fountain

summary: Three further separately registered St Anne’s Park landscape features were added after comparison against the archive: Herculanean Temple (50030024), rustic archway (50030030) and Yew Circle / former fountain (50030031).

title: St Anne’s Park — earlier walled garden, Rockwork Bridge, relocated gate screen and hermitage bridge

title: St Anne’s Park — holy well, pond temple and three Naniken bridges
status_label: FIVE FEATURES DOCUMENTED FROM OFFICIAL RECORDS
summary: Batch 135 adds the separately registered pond temple folly (NIAH 50030032), three distinct Naniken River/path bridges (NIAH 50030025, 50030027 and 50030036), and St Anne’s Well (RMP DU019-012), supported by an archaeological monitoring report.
supported: NIAH 50030032 describes a c.1860 single-bay temple folly overlooking an artificial pond, distinct from the already catalogued Herculanean Temple (50030024).
NIAH 50030025 records a c.1860 segmental-arch bridge with a carved stone bracket on the west spandrel and brick soffit visible at the path surface.
NIAH 50030027 records a separate c.1860 segmental-arch bridge with squared-stone voussoirs, part of the historic garden path system.

limits: The NIAH Irish Grid references for the four built structures are retained without WGS84 coordinates or founder GPS.
The well's published latitude/longitude and ITM coordinates are source-derived from the archaeological report, not field-verified.

Current condition, exact visibility of internal details and safe photographic viewpoints require field inspection.

title: St Anne’s Park — mansion archaeology, Rockwork Feature and Boathouse identity
status_label: ONE ARCHAEOLOGICAL RECORD VERIFIED; ONE LANDSCAPE LEAD PENDING FIELD IDENTIFICATION
summary: Batch 136 adds the excavated remains of St Anne’s House as a distinct archaeological site record, registers the Rockwork Feature as a research lead separate from Rockwork Bridge, and improves the existing NIAH 50030032 record by confirming its alternate identity as the Boathouse / Pompeiian Temple.
supported: Dublin City Council's 20 November 2024 archaeological report documents the 2024 excavation of 450 m² around the mansion's southern façade, portico, porch, picture gallery and part of the main hall.

The report records in-situ walls, surfaces, window recesses, portico foundations, surviving front-step details, decorative encaustic floor tiles, heating infrastructure and the historic carriage-road surface.
Dublin City Council's official follies list names both Rockwork Feature and Boat House as separate items in the park's twelve-folly group.

Oldstone Conservation's project account lists Rockwork Feature separately and identifies the Boathouse as the Pompeiian Temple, formerly used as a tea house. This supports aliasing the Boathouse to existing NIAH 50030032, not creating a duplicate.
limits: No WGS84 point is assigned to the mansion remains or Rockwork Feature; the report map and park-wide address are not precise enough for a feature pin.
Rockwork Feature remains RESEARCH_LEAD until its exact field location is positively identified; it is not the same object as Rockwork Bridge (NIAH 50030028).
The possible Lough Corrib origin of some boulders is a contractor's suggestion and is not accepted as verified provenance.
The excavation report documents discoveries and condition during 2024; current exposure, access and condition require fresh field verification.
The Boathouse alias is attached to existing NIAH 50030032 to avoid duplicate catalogue records.
